nodes.label: A0 · Elder tradition
nodes.definition: Organised reciprocity on this continent is older than the Republic. Indigenous nations ran complete economies of mutual obligation, and the United States tried to outlaw them by name.

argument.warrant: If the practice was old and functioning, and the state's own documents say it was suppressed because communal obligation stood in the way of self-interest, the contest between the two accounts is the oldest legal conflict on the continent.
argument.qualifier: This page does not claim Indigenous reciprocity as a chapter of the American civic tradition. It precedes that tradition.
argument.rebuttal: The bans were about religion and public order, not economics.
argument.answer: Teller condemned the feasts through which property was given away; Dawes named selfishness as the foundation the Cherokee lacked. The economic motive is the stated rationale.

nodes.label: A1 · Parallel founding of 1787
nodes.definition: Organised mutual aid in the United States is as old as the constitutional Republic. The Free African Society, 1787, Philadelphia, is the earliest documented formally organised network.

argument.warrant: The simultaneous founding of the Convention and the FAS in the same city, the same year, establishes mutual aid as a parallel founding act, not a later response.
argument.qualifier: Earliest documented formally organised network; older informal and Indigenous traditions precede it.
argument.rebuttal: The FAS was a small local organisation, not a national tradition.
argument.answer: Traditions begin somewhere. The Convention was also a small gathering in one city.

nodes.label: A2 · Parallel civic infrastructure
nodes.definition: Excluded communities built mutual aid as the primary social safety net — healthcare, insurance, burial, education — that the state and market denied them.

grounds: The Free African Society's design — dues, sickness benefits, burial provision — repeated in Charleston's Brown Fellowship Society (1790) and the New York African Society for Mutual Relief (1808).
Chinese huiguan consolidated as the Six Companies, Jewish landsmanshaftn, Italian società di mutuo soccorso, and Mexican sociedades mutualistas each independently built the same institution.
Du Bois's 1907 survey documented these organisations in the thousands as the principal provider of insurance, healthcare, education, and burial for Black Americans.
Public relief before the New Deal was local, discretionary, and racially exclusionary, so the societies were the system, not a supplement to it.
argument.warrant: If the same institutional design appears independently wherever exclusion created the same need, the pattern is structural: excluded communities built the safety net because no one else would.
argument.qualifier: Coverage varied by city and era; the societies did not reach everyone, and some enforced their own exclusions.
argument.rebuttal: These were private ethnic clubs, not civic infrastructure.
argument.answer: They performed the functions we now call the safety net — insurance, healthcare, burial, education — at documented scale, for communities the public system excluded by design.

nodes.label: A3 · Fraternal scale
nodes.definition: By 1920 roughly one in three adult American men belonged to a fraternal order that paid sickness, death, and burial benefits — the largest voluntary association system after the churches.

nodes.label: B1 · New Deal displacement
nodes.definition: New Deal social insurance replaced community provision and was narrated as filling a vacuum, not as taking over what lodges already did.

nodes.label: B2 · Civil rights care
nodes.definition: The Civil Rights movement ran on care infrastructure: citizenship schools, church networks, and provision that made sustained protest possible.

nodes.label: B3 · Survival programs
nodes.definition: The Black Panther survival programs — breakfast first among them — were mutual aid at civic scale, then watched, disrupted, and later absorbed as state policy.

nodes.label: B4 · AIDS networks
nodes.definition: During the AIDS crisis, care networks kept people alive when official medicine and the state would not.

nodes.label: B5 · Maternal networks
nodes.definition: The most pervasive form of mutual aid is maternal and kin care, and it has never been counted as civic infrastructure.

nodes.label: C1 · Crisis expansion
nodes.definition: In disaster, mutual aid routinely crosses the lines that bound it in ordinary time.

nodes.label: C2 · Labour across lines
nodes.definition: Labour organising built mutual aid across ethnic lines, not only inside them.

nodes.label: C3 · Institutions for everyone
nodes.definition: Some care institutions were deliberately built to serve beyond a single origin group.

nodes.label: C4 · Exclusion, not principle
nodes.definition: Ethnic boundedness of many societies reflected the exclusion they were answering, not a principle that care is only for one's own.

nodes.label: D1 · Legal undermining
nodes.definition: Tax, food-sharing, and disaster rules actively undermine reciprocal aid while privileging registered charity.

nodes.label: D2 · Competing tradition
nodes.definition: A funded civic-nationalist tradition claimed the definition of American and pushed mutual aid out of the centre of the story.

nodes.label: D3 · Project 2025
nodes.definition: Project 2025 is the current culmination of that displacing tradition: eligibility, compliance, and a narrowed circle of care written as policy.

nodes.label: D4 · Contestation
nodes.definition: The archive exists to contest that displacement by making the practice account citable civic knowledge.

nodes.label: Two accounts of belonging
nodes.definition: Belonging as practice (you are part of the community you show up for) versus belonging as condition (you belong if you qualify).

nodes.label: COMMUNITY IS FABRIC
nodes.definition: Community is woven, not bounded. Weakness requires more weaving, not cutting threads.

nodes.label: BELONGING IS SHOWING UP
nodes.definition: You belong by what you do, not by what you are.

nodes.label: HELP IS SUPPORT
nodes.definition: Care is structural reinforcement. Helping strengthens the whole.
nodes.source: SUPPORT image schema (Lakoff & Johnson) — project reframe

nodes.label: CARE IS BUILDING
nodes.definition: Care work produces infrastructure rather than depleting a scarce resource.

nodes.label: SOLIDARITY IS STANDING TOGETHER
nodes.definition: Shared practice and proximity are commitment.

nodes.label: NATION IS CONTAINER
nodes.definition: The nation is a bounded vessel. Care is for those inside. Exclusion looks like geography.
nodes.source: Lakoff & Johnson 1980 (container schema); Lakoff, Moral Politics 1996

nodes.label: MORALITY IS ACCOUNTING
nodes.definition: Moral worth is a balance sheet. Care is a withdrawal you must have paid in for.

nodes.label: CARE IS EXCHANGE
nodes.definition: Care is a commodity. Receiving without paying is freeloading.

nodes.label: CARE IS CHARITY
nodes.definition: Care flows one way, from benefactor to beneficiary. Reciprocal obligation is invisible.
nodes.source: Conventional cultural model, named in the Phase 1 linguistic reframe

nodes.label: CARE IS A SCARCE RESOURCE
nodes.definition: Care is finite and zero-sum. Exclusion reads as rationing.
nodes.source: Zero-sum resource metaphor — Phase 1 linguistic reframe

nodes.label: Collaboration
nodes.definition: Partners work together. No benefactor. Roles are reciprocal.

nodes.label: Building
nodes.definition: An agent creates a structure from components. Care as construction.

nodes.label: Eligibility
nodes.definition: Access depends on meeting criteria. Naming it activates gating.
nodes.source: FrameNet-style gating frame — Phase 1 frame inventory

nodes.label: Compliance
nodes.definition: A party must satisfy a rule to remain in good standing.

nodes.label: Crisis response
nodes.definition: Neighbours organise when the official system lags. Opens the reframe without a partisan argument.
nodes.source: Project catalytic frame — Phase 1 listening model

nodes.label: Tradition
nodes.definition: A practice is old and repeated. 'We always have.'
nodes.source: FrameNet: Custom — catalytic use per Phase 1 listening model

nodes.label: A · Founding tradition
nodes.definition: Mutual aid is a founding American tradition: present at the founding, built as civic infrastructure, and operating at national scale by 1920.

nodes.label: B · Survival through American identity
nodes.definition: The tradition survived the twentieth century by carrying excluded communities through crises the state and market would not meet.

nodes.label: C · Not only in-group
nodes.definition: The practice repeatedly crossed group lines; where it was bounded, the boundary reflected exclusion, not a principle of care for one’s own only.

nodes.label: D · Displacement and contest
nodes.definition: A funded rival account displaced mutual aid from the American story, and that displacement is contestable in the present.
